title: Sell Mineral Rights in Park County, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Park County, WY
metaDescription: Minerals under the Oregon Basin, Elk Basin, or Garland fields in Park County? Talk to a landman who reads Bighorn Basin division orders every week.
heroLead: Cody is the county seat, and the fields around it — Oregon Basin, Elk Basin, Garland — have been producing since the early 1900s. Park County minerals are usually well-documented; the question is whether the offer on the table reflects that.
intro: Park County sits on the western edge of the Bighorn Basin, up against the Absaroka Range and Yellowstone's east entrance. The oil history here runs deep — Oregon Basin field south of Cody has produced continuously for over a century, and Elk Basin straddling the Montana line has done the same. These are heavy, structurally complex fields with production out of the Tensleep, Phosphoria, and Frontier formations, mostly on long-established secondary and tertiary recovery programs rather than new wildcat drilling.

That history matters for a mineral owner because it means most Park County interests have decades of production data behind them. There is less guessing involved than in a newly leased county — the decline curve is a known quantity, division orders have been running steady, and county clerk records in Cody go back generations. We can usually move faster on a Park County file because the paper trail already exists.

sections.heading: Oregon Basin and the older fields around Cody
paragraphs: Oregon Basin is a heavily faulted anticline that has been through multiple phases of development — primary production, waterflood, and in parts, more advanced recovery. Owners here typically hold interests that have paid consistently for a long time, sometimes at a modest rate that reflects a mature field rather than a boom-year unit. If your minerals sit under Oregon Basin, Garland, or one of the other legacy Bighorn Basin structures near Cody, the offer we put together leans on that long production history rather than speculation about future drilling.

sections.heading: Split estate on ranch and irrigated ground
paragraphs: The Bighorn Basin around Powell and Cody has a lot of irrigated farm and ranch ground fed by the Shoshone Reclamation Project, and a fair amount of it has mineral rights that were reserved separately when homestead or ranch land changed hands decades ago. That is a classic split estate — the family farming the surface today may not be the family that owns what is underneath. If you inherited a fractional interest and are not sure whether it is tied to active production, Park County's clerk of court and assessor's office keep records that let us trace the severance and match it to the current well or unit.

sections.heading: Heirship and small fractional interests
paragraphs: A lot of what we buy in Park County is heirship interest — minerals that passed through two or three generations of a ranching or homesteading family without ever being consolidated. By the time it reaches you, your share might be a sixteenth or a sixty-fourth of the original tract. Selling a small fraction like that does not require you to track down every cousin who holds the rest of it; we buy what you own, and each owner's interest is a separate transaction under Wyoming law.

sections.heading: How we value a Park County interest
paragraphs: We start with the well or unit your interest sits in, your decimal share from the division order, and the production history the operator has filed with the state. Because most Park County production is mature and well-documented through the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, we can usually verify the decline curve quickly and price against it rather than against a rough estimate. Any number we give you is tied to that record, not a flat per-acre figure pulled out of the air.

faqs.question: My interest is under an old field near Cody that's been producing for decades. Is it still worth anything to sell?
faqs.answer: Often, yes — a long, stable production history is easier to price with confidence than a brand-new well, so mature Bighorn Basin interests are some of the more straightforward files we work.

faqs.question: How do I find out which well or unit my minerals are in?
faqs.answer: Your division order or check stub will list the well name and your decimal interest. If you don't have one, give us the legal description and we can trace it through Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission records.

faqs.question: I only inherited a small fraction of the original family interest. Can I still sell just my share?
faqs.answer: Yes. Wyoming mineral interests are commonly split among heirs, and each owner's fractional share is its own asset. You do not need the other heirs to sell alongside you.

faqs.question: Is my mineral interest separate from the ranch or farm ground it sits under?
faqs.answer: It can be. Reclamation-era irrigated land in Park County was often sold with the minerals reserved separately. We check clerk of court deed records to confirm the severance before we make an offer.

faqs.question: Does secondary recovery or waterflood activity change what my interest is worth?
faqs.answer: It can extend a field's productive life and stabilize the decline, which we factor into valuation. It's part of why mature Park County fields often price differently than a newly drilled county.
